passage:
Dear Sharmila,

I owe you and the team an apology. For two weeks I told myself I was saving time by doing the project alone. I stayed up until two most nights cutting, gluing and writing the report, because I thought nobody else would do it right. By Thursday my eyes were burning and I got the scale wrong on the base. Nobody noticed, because nobody had been asked. You offered to help twice and I said, "It's fine." I know that must have made you feel unneeded. The model looks rough now, and none of you knows it well enough to explain it. I made it worse by refusing help. Can we sit down on Monday and split up what's left?

Akash

qa.q: Until what time did Akash stay up on most nights?
qa.a: Akash stayed up until two on most nights.

qa.q: How does Akash feel now about refusing help?
qa.a: Akash feels regretful and worn out, admitting the refusal made things worse and left the team unable to explain the model.

qa.q: What could Akash have done instead of working alone, and why?
qa.a: Akash could have split the tasks at the start and checked in on progress, because shared work keeps quality up and lets everyone learn.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have felt when the offers of help were turned down?
qa.a: Sharmila probably felt sidelined and unneeded, since two offers of help were refused with 'It's fine.'

grounding: Not trusting others, the leader does most of the work at night and gets exhausted, the team feels sidelined, the quality drops and members learn nothing from the project.

passage:
You want to know about the history project, Uday? Fine. It's not a proud story.

I'm Ritu, and I was made group leader for a model of the Harappan city. Four of us. On day one I looked at everyone's rough sketches and thought, these are messy, I'll just do it myself.

So I did. Every night for two weeks I was up till one, cutting cardboard, painting drains, writing the chart. In class I told the others, "It's handled, relax."

By the last week I was falling asleep in maths. My hands shook when I glued the roofs. The drains I painted at 2 am were crooked.

We got a C. And the worst part was at the viva: the teacher asked the others how the drainage worked, and they couldn't answer. They'd never touched it. One of them said, "Ritu didn't let us."

qa.q: What grade did the model get?
How did Ritu seem to feel when a teammate said "Ritu didn't let us"?
qa.a: Ritu felt ashamed and stung, realising the others had been shut out rather than lazy.

qa.q: What approach could Ritu have used instead of doing it all alone?
qa.a: Ritu could have given each person one part with a check-in to review quality, so work was shared and everyone learned the drainage system.

qa.q: How did the project look to the other three members?
qa.a: They likely felt sidelined and a little resentful, unable to answer at the viva because they were never allowed to touch the work.

grounding: A spoken account of a leader who does most of the work alone at night, becomes exhausted, lowers quality and leaves the team sidelined and unable to learn.

passage:
I'm Tanvir, Simran's neighbour in the hostel. For three weeks before our Class 11 geography project was due, her light was on past midnight almost every night. I could see it under the door.

Once I knocked to borrow a charger. Her desk was covered in maps, glue and three laptops' worth of printouts. "Where's your group?" I asked. "Sleeping. It's faster if I do it," she said, not looking up.

In the mess, her group members sat together laughing. When a teacher asked one of them about the rainfall chart, the girl shrugged and said, "Simran's doing that."

The day before submission, Simran came to breakfast with red eyes and dropped her plate. The model looked fine from far away, but the labels were misspelt.

I don't know how she felt. She didn't talk much that week.

qa.q: What did the girl in Simran's group say about the rainfall chart?
qa.a: She shrugged and said, "Simran's doing that."

qa.q: What might Simran have been feeling the morning she dropped her plate?
qa.a: She was probably exhausted and strained, and perhaps anxious or low, since she had been up past midnight for weeks and grew quiet afterwards.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Simran led the group?
qa.a: Hand real parts of the work to the group with a short daily review, so she is not up all night and the others actually learn the geography.

qa.q: How did the project look to Tanvir from next door?
qa.a: To Tanvir it looked like one person carrying everything while the group relaxed, though Tanvir admits not knowing how Simran felt.

grounding: An observer describes a leader who does most of the project work alone at night, grows exhausted and leaves the team sidelined.
